hypotheses.title: Anyone can call initialize() on the vault proxy to seize ownership
hypotheses.description: The vault is deployed behind an ERC1967 proxy, but `initialize` is a public function guarded only by OpenZeppelin's `initializer` modifier. If the proxy is deployed and `initialize` is not called atomically in the same transaction (a common deployment pattern), any external actor can front-run the legitimate initialization and become the owner. The attacker then controls `onlyOwner` functions including `upgradeTo`, `setVaultActive`, `setMinimumDepositAmount`, and can also set themselves as investment manager.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Deployer deploys the ERC1967 proxy pointing at the implementation. 2) Before the deployer's `initialize` transaction lands, attacker calls `initialize(asset, shareToken, attacker)` with valid non-zero arguments. 3) `initializer` modifier passes because it has not been consumed. 4) Attacker becomes owner and investment manager. 5) Attacker calls `upgradeTo(maliciousImpl)` to fully take over the vault, or drains via `investAssets`/`withdrawFromInvestment` once configured.
hypotheses.impact: Complete takeover of the vault proxy: attacker can upgrade to arbitrary implementation, drain assets, or brick the vault. Loss of all user funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Deploy and initialize atomically (e.g., via a factory that calls `initialize` in the same tx as proxy creation), or add an `_initialized` check plus a deployer-only bootstrap guard.

hypotheses.title: fulfillDeposit/fulfillRedeem can be permanently blocked by investment manager
hypotheses.description: `fulfillDeposit`, `fulfillRedeem`, `fulfillCancelDepositRequest`, and `fulfillCancelRedeemRequest` are all gated by `msg.sender != $.investmentManager`. If the investment manager is set to a non-functional address (e.g., a contract that cannot call, or a lost key), all pending requests are permanently stuck in Pending state. Users cannot cancel their own pending requests to recover funds — `cancelDepositRequest` moves assets to `pendingCancelDepositAssets`, but `fulfillCancelDepositRequest` (also manager-only) is required before `claimCancelDepositRequest` can succeed. So even cancelation is blocked.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. User calls `requestDeposit(assets, controller, owner)` — assets transferred to vault, state set to pending. 2. Investment manager is set to a dead address (or is compromised/offline). 3. User calls `cancelDepositRequest(0, controller)` — succeeds, moves to `pendingCancelDepositAssets`. 4. User calls `claimCancelDepositRequest(0, receiver, controller)` — reverts with `CancelationNotClaimable` because `claimableCancelDepositAssets[controller] == 0`. 5. User's assets are stuck in the vault forever.
hypotheses.impact: User assets are permanently locked in the vault. No user-initiated recovery path exists for pending deposits or redeems.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow users to claim back their pending deposits directly after a timeout without manager fulfillment, or allow cancelation to short-circuit to claimable after a delay.

hypotheses.title: WERC7575Vault._withdraw burns shares without verifying caller authorization
hypotheses.description: `_withdraw` calls `_shareToken.spendSelfAllowance(owner, shares)` and then `_shareToken.burn(owner, shares)`. `spendSelfAllowance` spends the owner's self-allowance (owner→owner), which is set via `permit` with a validator signature. However, `_withdraw` never checks that `msg.sender == owner` or that `msg.sender` has any allowance from `owner`. Any external caller can invoke `withdraw`/`redeem` with an arbitrary `owner` address, and as long as the owner has previously set a self-allowance (which is required for any transfer in this token), the caller can burn the owner's shares and redirect the assets to any `receiver`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim has a self-allowance on the share token (required for them to transfer at all). 2) Attacker calls `WERC7575Vault.withdraw(assets, attacker, victim)` or `redeem(shares, attacker, victim)`. 3) `_withdraw` calls `spendSelfAllowance(victim, shares)` which succeeds because the victim's self-allowance is set. 4) Shares are burned from victim and assets are sent to attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Any user with a self-allowance can have their shares burned and assets stolen by any external caller. Complete loss of funds for affected users.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `_withdraw`, require `msg.sender == owner` or verify an explicit allowance from `owner` to `msg.sender` (not self-allowance) before burning.

hypotheses.title: fulfillRedeem uses current exchange rate, not request-time rate
hypotheses.description: When a user submits requestRedeem, the shares are locked but no asset amount is recorded. The investment manager later calls fulfillRedeem which computes assets = _convertToAssets(shares, Floor) using the CURRENT exchange rate (which depends on totalAssets() and circulating supply at that moment). Since the manager controls when to fulfill and can also invest/withdraw assets (changing totalAssets), the manager can time fulfillment to give the user fewer assets than the shares were worth at request time. The user has no protection because the rate is not snapshotted at requestRedeem.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User calls requestRedeem(1000 shares). 2) Manager waits, then calls investAssets to move idle assets into investment vault, reducing totalAssets() (since invested assets are excluded from totalAssets). 3) Manager calls fulfillRedeem — _convertToAssets now returns a much smaller asset amount because totalNormalizedAssets dropped. 4) User receives fewer assets than fair value; manager/investment vault captures the difference.
hypotheses.impact: Users redeeming shares receive less than the fair value of their shares; value is transferred to the investment vault/manager. Systematic loss of user funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot the exchange rate (or the normalized asset amount) at requestRedeem time and use that stored rate in fulfillRedeem, or require fulfillment within a bounded window with a rate oracle.

hypotheses.title: Share price manipulation via direct asset donation to vault
hypotheses.description: The share price is computed as `totalNormalizedAssets / circulatingSupply` where `totalNormalizedAssets` is derived from each vault's `totalAssets()`, which is simply `IERC20(asset).balanceOf(vault) - reserved`. Any external actor can transfer assets directly to a vault contract (or to the investment ShareToken) to inflate `totalNormalizedAssets` without minting shares. Because `fulfillDeposit` and `fulfillRedeem` use this ratio to convert between assets and shares, an attacker can manipulate the conversion rate at the moment a pending request is fulfilled.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker submits a large `requestDeposit` (or waits for a victim's pending request). 2) Attacker directly transfers a large amount of the underlying asset to the vault contract (or to the investment ShareToken address) via `IERC20.transfer`, which is not blocked. 3) `totalAssets()` now reports an inflated value, so `convertNormalizedAssetsToShares` returns fewer shares per asset. 4) When the investment manager calls `fulfillDeposit` for the victim (or the attacker's own request), the victim receives fewer shares than expected, and the attacker can later redeem at the inflated rate. 5) Attacker can also front-run `fulfillRedeem` to inflate the asset payout per share.
hypotheses.impact: Victims receive fewer shares on deposit or fewer assets on redeem; attacker extracts value from other users' pending requests. Direct loss of funds and broken accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track vault assets via internal accounting (e.g., a `totalManagedAssets` variable updated only on deposit/withdraw/invest) instead of `balanceOf`, or use a virtual-offset / donation-resistant share price mechanism.

hypotheses.title: Vault pause traps user funds with no recovery path
hypotheses.description: `pause()` sets the Pausable state, and `deposit`, `mint`, `withdraw`, `redeem` all have `whenNotPaused`. Critically, `_withdraw` calls `_shareToken.burn(owner, shares)` and `_shareToken.spendSelfAllowance(owner, shares)`, both of which are `whenNotPaused` on the ShareToken. So even if the vault were unpaused, the ShareToken pause blocks burns. There is no emergency withdrawal function that bypasses pause. Once paused, users cannot redeem their shares for assets, and the assets remain locked in the vault.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Owner calls `pause()` on the vault (or on the ShareToken). 2. User calls `redeem(shares, receiver, owner)` — reverts due to `whenNotPaused`. 3. User calls `withdraw(assets, receiver, owner)` — reverts due to `whenNotPaused`. 4. User has no alternative function to retrieve assets. 5. Funds are stuck until owner unpauses.
hypotheses.impact: User assets are frozen indefinitely if the owner never unpauses (e.g., lost key, malicious owner, or governance deadlock). No user-initiated recovery.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an emergency withdrawal path that allows users to redeem their pro-rata share even when paused, or document that pause is temporary and add a timelock.

hypotheses.title: setInvestmentManager callable by shareToken allows arbitrary manager takeover
hypotheses.description: `setInvestmentManager` allows either `owner()` OR `$.shareToken` to set the investment manager. The share token is a separate contract whose owner can call `ShareTokenUpgradeable.setInvestmentManager`, which then calls `ERC7575VaultUpgradeable(vault).setInvestmentManager(newManager)` on every registered vault. This means the share token owner (a distinct trust domain from the vault owner) can unilaterally replace the vault's investment manager. The investment manager can call `fulfillDeposit`, `fulfillRedeem`, `investAssets`, and `withdrawFromInvestment`, giving it control over asset flows.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker compromises or is the share token owner (or the share token is upgraded to a malicious implementation). 2) Attacker calls `ShareTokenUpgradeable.setInvestmentManager(attacker)`. 3) This propagates to every registered vault via `setInvestmentManager`. 4) Attacker as investment manager calls `investAssets` to route vault assets into an attacker-controlled investment vault, or manipulates `fulfillRedeem`/`fulfillDeposit` conversions.
hypotheses.impact: Vault assets can be redirected or mispriced by an actor outside the vault's own ownership. Loss of funds or accounting corruption across all registered vaults.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the `$.shareToken` branch from `setInvestmentManager` (and `setInvestmentVault`), or require both owner and share token to agree (e.g., two-step confirmation).

hypotheses.title: setInvestmentVault callable by shareToken allows arbitrary vault redirection
hypotheses.description: `setInvestmentVault` accepts callers that are either `owner()` or `$.shareToken`. The share token owner can therefore set the investment vault on any registered vault. The only validation is that `investmentVault_.asset() == $.asset`. An attacker-controlled contract that returns the correct asset address from `asset()` will pass validation. Once set, `investAssets` will approve and deposit vault assets into this attacker-controlled contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (share token owner or via malicious share token upgrade) deploys a fake investment vault whose `asset()` returns the correct asset and whose `deposit()` steals the transferred assets. 2) Attacker calls `setInvestmentVault(fakeVault)` on the target vault (allowed because msg.sender == shareToken). 3) Attacker (as investment manager, set via the same trust path) calls `investAssets(amount)`. 4) Vault approves and transfers assets to the fake vault, which keeps them.
hypotheses.impact: Direct theft of vault assets via a malicious investment vault. Loss of user funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `setInvestmentVault` to `onlyOwner` on the vault itself, or require the investment vault to be registered/validated by the share token's own registry.

hypotheses.title: fulfillDeposit uses current rate, allowing manager to dilute depositors
hypotheses.description: requestDeposit locks assets but records no share amount. fulfillDeposit computes shares = _convertToShares(assets, Floor) using the current exchange rate. The investment manager controls both when to fulfill and the vault's totalAssets() via investAssets/withdrawFromInvestment. By manipulating totalAssets before fulfilling, the manager can mint more or fewer shares than the depositor should receive, diluting existing holders or shortchanging the depositor.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User requests deposit of 1000 USDC. 2) Manager calls withdrawFromInvestment to inflate totalAssets() (or investAssets to deflate). 3) Manager calls fulfillDeposit — shares minted are computed at the manipulated rate. 4) If rate was inflated, user gets fewer shares; the surplus value accrues to existing holders (including manager-controlled accounts).
hypotheses.impact: Depositors receive incorrect share amounts; existing holders can be diluted or enriched at the expense of new depositors. Wrong accounting of share supply vs assets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot the exchange rate at requestDeposit time and use it in fulfillDeposit, or restrict manager's ability to change totalAssets between request and fulfillment.

hypotheses.title: fulfillRedeem uses manipulable share price at fulfillment time
hypotheses.category: Price used before it is updated / spot-price manipulation
hypotheses.description: `fulfillRedeem` computes `assets = _convertToAssets(shares, Floor)` using the current share price derived from `ShareTokenUpgradeable.getCirculatingSupplyAndAssets()`, which depends on live vault balances and the investment ShareToken balance. The investment manager (or anyone who can influence the price via direct transfers) can move the price between the user's `requestRedeem` and the manager's `fulfillRedeem`, so the assets credited to the controller are not the assets that were economically owed at request time. There is no stored price or slippage bound.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim calls `requestRedeem(shares)`. 2) Attacker (or a colluding manager) directly transfers assets out of / into the vault or investment ShareToken to move the share price. 3) Manager calls `fulfillRedeem` at the manipulated price, crediting the victim with fewer assets than the shares were worth at request time. 4) Attacker redeems their own shares at the favorable price.
hypotheses.impact: Redeemers receive less than fair value; value is transferred to the attacker/manager. Loss of funds and unfair accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot the conversion rate at `requestRedeem` time (or use a TWAP/oracle) and use that stored rate in `fulfillRedeem`, or enforce a minimum-out parameter supplied by the controller.

hypotheses.title: fulfillDeposit mints shares at manipulable price with no slippage bound
hypotheses.description: `fulfillDeposit` converts pending assets to shares using the live share price from `ShareTokenUpgradeable.convertNormalizedAssetsToShares`, which is derived from current vault balances and the investment ShareToken balance. The depositor has no way to specify a minimum acceptable share amount, and the manager can fulfill at any time. An attacker who can move the price (via direct transfers to the vault or investment ShareToken) can cause the depositor to receive fewer shares than expected.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim calls `requestDeposit(assets)`. 2) Attacker inflates `totalNormalizedAssets` by transferring assets directly to the vault or investment ShareToken. 3) Manager calls `fulfillDeposit`; victim receives fewer shares than the assets were worth at request time. 4) Attacker redeems at the inflated price.
hypotheses.impact: Depositors receive fewer shares than fair value; value extracted by attacker. Loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a `minShares` parameter to `requestDeposit`/`fulfillDeposit` and revert if the computed shares are below it, or snapshot the price at request time.

hypotheses.title: Read-only reentrancy in getCirculatingSupplyAndAssets via vault callbacks
hypotheses.description: `getCirculatingSupplyAndAssets()` iterates over registered vaults and calls `getClaimableSharesAndNormalizedAssets()` on each, which in turn calls `totalAssets()` on the vault. `totalAssets()` reads the vault's asset balance and subtracts reserved amounts. During a redeem/withdraw flow in `ERC7575VaultUpgradeable`, the vault burns shares and then transfers assets to the receiver; if the asset token has a callback (ERC-777 style) or the receiver is a contract that re-enters, the vault's balance and `totalClaimableRedeemAssets`/`totalClaimableRedeemShares` are in an inconsistent intermediate state. Any external protocol that reads `convertNormalizedAssetsToShares`/`convertSharesToNormalizedAssets` (which call `getCirculatingSupplyAndAssets`) during that window sees a manipulated share price.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious asset token with a transfer hook (or uses an ERC-777-like asset) and registers a vault. 2) Attacker calls `redeem()` on the vault; during `SafeTokenTransfers.safeTransfer` the asset's hook re-enters an external protocol that queries `ShareTokenUpgradeable.convertSharesToNormalizedAssets` or `getCirculatingSupplyAndAssets`. 3) At that moment `totalClaimableRedeemShares` has already been decremented but the asset balance has not yet left the vault (or vice versa depending on ordering), so `totalNormalizedAssets` and `circulatingSupply` are skewed. 4) Attacker uses the skewed price to mint/redeem at favorable rates in the same transaction.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect share/asset pricing leading to theft of value from other users, insolvency of the vault, or wrong accounting in any integrator relying on the conversion functions.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard to the view path or compute circulating supply/assets from cached snapshots that are updated atomically before external transfers; alternatively, perform all state updates (including `totalClaimableRedeemAssets`/`Shares`) strictly before any external token transfer and document that integrators must not read during transfers.

hypotheses.title: KYC admin can permanently freeze all user transfers via KYC revocation
hypotheses.description: `transfer()` and `transferFrom()` require `isKycVerified[to]` to be true, and `mint`/`burn` also require KYC on the target. The KYC admin can revoke KYC at any time, which immediately blocks the user from transferring shares out, and also blocks vault `burn`/`mint` operations that touch that user (e.g., `redeem`/`withdraw` in the vault call `burn(address(this), shares)` — but the vault itself must be KYC-verified, and the user's shares are held by the vault, so the user's own KYC status is not directly checked on redeem). However, the user's own `transfer` to any receiver requires the receiver to be KYC-verified, and the user's own shares cannot be moved if the user is not KYC-verified because `_spendAllowance(from, from, value)` is called on the user's own allowance — but the KYC check is only on `to`. The real trap: once KYC is revoked for a user, they cannot transfer shares to anyone (since `to` must be KYC-verified, and the user themselves cannot be a valid `to` for a self-transfer because `approve` blocks self-approval and `permit` requires validator signature). Combined with `pause()`, the owner can freeze all share movement.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. KYC admin (or owner who controls KYC admin) revokes KYC for a user. 2. User attempts `transfer(to, amount)` — reverts with `KycRequired` if `to` is not KYC-verified. 3. User attempts to redeem via vault — vault calls `burn(address(this), shares)` which requires `isKycVerified[address(this)]` (the vault), not the user, so this may still work. But the user cannot move shares to any non-KYC address, and cannot self-approve to enable `transfer` to themselves. 4. Owner calls `pause()` — all `transfer`, `transferFrom`, `mint`, `burn` revert. 5. User's shares are stuck: cannot transfer, cannot redeem (vault `burn` reverts due to pause), cannot withdraw.
hypotheses.impact: User funds (shares) are permanently frozen. No recovery path exists for the user — only the owner/KYC admin can unfreeze by re-verifying KYC and unpausing.
hypotheses.recommendation: Provide a permissionless escape hatch (e.g., allow users to redeem directly to themselves bypassing KYC on `to` when `to == msg.sender`, or allow burning without KYC check when the vault is the caller and the user is the owner).

hypotheses.title: transferFrom double-spends allowance: owner self-allowance AND caller allowance
hypotheses.description: `transferFrom(from, to, value)` calls `_spendAllowance(from, from, value)` (spending owner's self-allowance) and then `super.transferFrom(from, to, value)` which internally calls `_spendAllowance(from, msg.sender, value)` (spending caller's allowance). This means every transferFrom consumes BOTH the owner's self-allowance AND the caller's allowance. The owner's self-allowance is a global resource required for ALL transfers (including the owner's own `transfer`). So any third party with a small allowance from the owner can drain the owner's self-allowance by calling transferFrom repeatedly, eventually blocking the owner's own transfers. This is a griefing/DoS attack.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Owner sets self-allowance via permit (required for any transfer). 2. Owner approves attacker for a small amount (e.g., 1 wei) via approve. 3. Attacker calls transferFrom(owner, attacker, 1) repeatedly. 4. Each call decrements owner's self-allowance by 1. 5. Owner's self-allowance reaches 0. 6. Owner's own `transfer` calls now revert with insufficient allowance. 7. Owner must re-permit (requires validator signature) to restore functionality.
hypotheses.impact: Owner's transfers are blocked (DoS) until re-permit. If validator is unavailable, owner's funds are frozen.
hypotheses.recommendation: In transferFrom, only spend the caller's allowance, not the owner's self-allowance. The self-allowance should only be spent by the owner's own `transfer`.

hypotheses.title: requestRedeem double-spends ERC20 allowance via spendAllowance + vaultTransferFrom
hypotheses.description: When msg.sender is not owner/operator, the vault calls `ShareTokenUpgradeable.spendAllowance(owner, msg.sender, shares)` to consume the ERC20 allowance, then calls `vaultTransferFrom(owner, address(this), shares)` which performs a direct `_transfer` without any allowance check. The allowance is consumed but the actual share movement bypasses the ERC20 allowance path entirely, so the same allowance can be reused across multiple requests if the owner's balance is replenished, and more importantly the vault's own `vaultTransferFrom` is not gated by the ERC20 allowance semantics the user expects.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a small ERC20 allowance from victim (e.g., 100 shares). 2) Attacker calls requestRedeem(100, attacker, victim) — allowance is spent, shares moved to vault. 3) Victim later approves again or attacker uses a different vault sharing the same ShareToken; because `vaultTransferFrom` bypasses allowance, any registered vault can move shares from any owner without allowance as long as the vault is registered. 4) Attacker registers/uses a malicious-but-registered vault (or exploits any vault) to drain victim shares via `vaultTransferFrom` without any allowance.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized transfer of user shares by any registered vault; loss of user funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the direct `vaultTransferFrom` bypass or require that the vault only moves shares after consuming allowance via `transferFrom`; do not expose an allowance-free transfer primitive to arbitrary registered vaults.

hypotheses.title: totalAssets() excludes claimableCancelDepositAssets, understating vault holdings
hypotheses.description: totalAssets() subtracts totalPendingDepositAssets, totalClaimableRedeemAssets, and totalCancelDepositAssets from the vault's token balance. However, claimableCancelDepositAssets (assets moved to claimable state after fulfillCancelDepositRequest) are NOT subtracted. These assets are still physically in the vault and are reserved for users to claim via claimCancelDepositRequest. Since they are not excluded, they are counted as "available" in totalAssets(), inflating the denominator used in convertToShares/convertToAssets. This means new depositors' shares are computed against assets that are actually reserved for cancelation claimants.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User A requests deposit, then cancels; manager fulfills cancelation, moving assets to claimableCancelDepositAssets. 2) totalAssets() still includes these assets. 3) User B requests deposit; manager fulfills at an inflated rate because totalAssets is overstated. 4) User B receives fewer shares than fair, or the vault becomes insolvent when User A claims their cancelation assets.
hypotheses.impact: Share pricing is wrong; new depositors are diluted or the vault becomes insolvent when cancelation claimants withdraw reserved assets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include claimableCancelDepositAssets in the reservedAssets subtraction in totalAssets().

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy in redeem/withdraw via asset transfer before event/state finalization
hypotheses.description: In `redeem()`, the vault decrements `claimableRedeemAssets`/`claimableRedeemShares`, decrements `totalClaimableRedeemAssets`/`totalClaimableRedeemShares`, burns shares, emits the event, and then calls `SafeTokenTransfers.safeTransfer` to send assets to the receiver. Although `nonReentrant` protects the vault's own entry points, the external asset transfer can call back into the ShareToken (e.g., `mint`/`burn` are `onlyVaults`, but `transfer`/`transferFrom` on the share token are callable) or into other vaults sharing the same ShareToken. Because `totalClaimableRedeemShares` has already been decremented while the asset has not yet left the vault, `getCirculatingSupplyAndAssets()` returns a distorted ratio during the callback window.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker uses an asset token with a transfer hook (or a receiver contract that re-enters). 2) Attacker calls `redeem()`; during `safeTransfer` the hook calls `ShareTokenUpgradeable.convertSharesToNormalizedAssets` or another vault's `requestDeposit`/`fulfillDeposit` path. 3) The distorted `circulatingSupply`/`totalNormalizedAssets` lets the attacker obtain more shares per asset (or more assets per share) than fair. 4) Attacker repeats or combines with a flash loan to extract value.
hypotheses.impact: Value extraction from other depositors, incorrect share minting, potential vault insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move the asset transfer to the very end after all state is finalized (already partially done) and ensure no view function used by integrators can be read mid-transfer; consider a global reentrancy lock on the ShareToken's conversion functions or snapshot-based pricing.

hypotheses.title: fulfillDeposit mints shares at current rate, not request-time rate
hypotheses.description: `fulfillDeposit` computes `shares = _convertToShares(assets, Floor)` using the current ShareToken exchange rate at fulfillment time. The investment manager chooses when to fulfill, so they can delay fulfillment until the rate is unfavorable to the depositor (fewer shares per asset) or favorable to themselves, extracting value from pending depositors.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User submits requestDeposit with assets. 2) Manager waits until `convertNormalizedAssetsToShares` yields fewer shares (e.g., by donating assets to another vault, or by calling `investAssets`/`withdrawFromInvestment` to shift `totalAssets`). 3) Manager calls fulfillDeposit, locking in the worse rate. 4) Manager fulfills their own deposits at a better rate.
hypotheses.impact: Depositors receive fewer shares than fair; value extracted by manager; inconsistent accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot the exchange rate at requestDeposit time and use it in fulfillDeposit, or enforce a bounded fulfillment window.

hypotheses.title: WERC7575ShareToken.transferFrom ignores caller allowance
hypotheses.description: `transferFrom(from, to, value)` calls `_spendAllowance(from, from, value)` — it spends the `from` account's self-allowance instead of the caller's allowance from `from`. It then calls `super.transferFrom(from, to, value)`, which in OZ ERC20 also spends `msg.sender`'s allowance from `from`. But the critical issue is that the self-allowance check is the only gate that matters for the custom token's semantics, and it does not bind the caller. Any external caller can move tokens from any `from` address that has a self-allowance set, to any `to` address, without holding any allowance from `from`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim sets a self-allowance (required for them to transfer at all). 2) Attacker calls `transferFrom(victim, attacker, amount)`. 3) `_spendAllowance(victim, victim, amount)` succeeds because victim's self-allowance is set. 4) `super.transferFrom` then attempts to spend attacker's allowance from victim — if attacker has none, OZ reverts. However, if the attacker first obtains any allowance (e.g., via a permit signed by victim for a tiny amount, or if the victim has approved the attacker for anything), the attacker can drain up to the self-allowance amount.
hypotheses.impact: Users who have set a self-allowance and any allowance to a third party can have their full balance drained by that third party, bypassing the intended per-allowance limits.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `transferFrom`, spend `msg.sender`'s allowance from `from` (standard ERC20 semantics) and do not rely on `from`'s self-allowance for third-party transfers.

hypotheses.title: withdraw() can burn zero shares while transferring assets
hypotheses.description: In withdraw(), shares = assets.mulDiv(availableShares, availableAssets, Floor). If availableShares < availableAssets (possible when share/asset ratio drifts due to rounding in fulfillRedeem), a small `assets` request can round shares down to 0. The code then skips the burn (if shares > 0) but still decrements totalClaimableRedeemShares by 0 and transfers `assets` to the receiver. The user extracts assets without burning any shares, and the vault's claimableRedeemShares for that controller is decremented by 0 while claimableRedeemAssets is decremented by assets — leaving the controller with claimable shares but no backing assets.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker accumulates claimableRedeemShares and claimableRedeemAssets where shares < assets (e.g., 1 share claimable for 2 assets due to prior rounding). 2) Attacker calls withdraw(1, receiver, controller) repeatedly. 3) shares = 1*1/2 = 0 (floor). 4) No burn occurs, but 1 asset is transferred and claimableRedeemAssets decremented. 5) Attacker drains all assets while keeping the shares, then can potentially redeem the shares again if any assets remain.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker extracts assets without burning shares, potentially draining the vault's claimable assets while retaining claimable shares — double-spend of the same claim.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert if shares == 0 in withdraw(), or require shares > 0 before allowing the asset transfer.

hypotheses.title: totalAssets excludes pending deposits but includes them in share price denominator
hypotheses.category: Wrong accounting / price used before it is updated
hypotheses.description: `totalAssets()` subtracts `totalPendingDepositAssets`, `totalClaimableRedeemAssets`, and `totalCancelDepositAssets` from the vault balance, but `ShareTokenUpgradeable.getCirculatingSupplyAndAssets()` adds `_calculateInvestmentAssets()` (the investment ShareToken balance) on top. Pending deposit assets are physically in the vault but excluded from `totalAssets`, while the shares that will be minted for them are not yet in circulation. This creates a window where the share price is artificially low (assets excluded, supply unchanged), and a subsequent `fulfillDeposit` mints shares at that low price. An attacker can exploit this by timing a large `requestDeposit` followed by a `fulfillDeposit` before other pending deposits are fulfilled.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `requestDeposit` with a large amount, increasing `totalPendingDepositAssets` and thus reducing `totalAssets()`. 2) Attacker (or manager) calls `fulfillDeposit` for the attacker's own request; shares are minted at the artificially low price. 3) Other pending deposits are fulfilled later at a higher price, diluting them. 4) Attacker redeems at the higher price.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker mints more shares than fair value; other depositors are diluted. Loss of funds and unfair accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include pending deposit assets in `totalAssets()` (or exclude them from the share price denominator consistently) so the price is not artificially depressed by pending requests.

hypotheses.title: requestRedeem spends allowance before balance check, allowing griefing via reentrancy
hypotheses.description: In `requestRedeem()`, when the caller is not owner/operator, `ShareTokenUpgradeable.spendAllowance(owner, msg.sender, shares)` is called before the balance check `IERC20Metadata($.shareToken).balanceOf(owner) < shares`. `spendAllowance` is an external call to the ShareToken. If the ShareToken's `_spendAllowance` were to trigger any callback (e.g., via a future upgrade or a malicious share token), the allowance would already be consumed while the balance check has not yet run. Even without a callback, the ordering means an attacker can front-run a legitimate owner's allowance consumption by calling `requestRedeem` with a large `shares` value that passes the allowance check but fails the balance check, consuming the allowance and reverting — a griefing vector.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim approves attacker (or an operator) with an allowance on the share token. 2) Attacker calls `requestRedeem(shares, controller, owner)` with `shares` equal to the allowance but greater than the owner's balance. 3) `spendAllowance` succeeds (consuming the allowance), then the balance check reverts. 4) The victim's allowance is now zero, blocking legitimate future redemptions until re-approved.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing — victim's allowance is consumed without a successful redemption; denial of service for legitimate redemption requests.
hypotheses.recommendation: Perform the balance check before calling `spendAllowance`, or use a pull-based allowance pattern that only consumes allowance after all checks pass.

hypotheses.title: getActiveDepositRequesters reverts when >100 requesters, breaking off-chain monitoring
hypotheses.description: `getActiveDepositRequesters()` and `getActiveRedeemRequesters()` revert with `TooManyRequesters` if the set length exceeds 100. Any untrusted user can call `requestDeposit` with a tiny amount (>= minimumDepositAmount) to add themselves to `activeDepositRequesters`. With 101 distinct addresses, the view function reverts, breaking any off-chain monitoring or integration that relies on it. The paginated alternatives exist, but any consumer using the non-paginated version is DoS'd.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deploys 101 addresses (or uses 101 EOAs). 2. Each calls `requestDeposit(minimumDepositAmount, self, self)` — each adds to `activeDepositRequesters`. 3. Any call to `getActiveDepositRequesters()` now reverts. 4. Off-chain dashboards, monitoring, or integrations that call this function break.
hypotheses.impact: Off-chain monitoring and integrations are broken. Not a direct fund loss, but a griefing vector that can break dependent systems.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the revert and return a truncated array, or always use the paginated version internally.

hypotheses.title: batchTransfers and rBatchTransfers do not check KYC for creditors
hypotheses.description: `batchTransfers` and `rBatchTransfers` update `_balances` directly without checking KYC for creditors. This allows the validator to transfer tokens to non-KYC addresses, bypassing the KYC requirement enforced in `transfer` and `transferFrom`. Since the validator is a trusted role, this is a trust assumption. But the validator could be compromised, or the validator could be tricked into including a non-KYC address. Medium severity.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Validator calls batchTransfers with a non-KYC creditor. 2. Tokens are credited to the non-KYC address. 3. Non-KYC address now holds tokens, bypassing KYC.
hypotheses.impact: KYC requirement is bypassed, allowing non-KYC users to hold tokens.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add KYC check for creditors in batchTransfers and rBatchTransfers.

hypotheses.title: Asymmetric rounding in deposit/mint lets users extract dust from other controllers
hypotheses.description: `fulfillDeposit` mints shares Floor-rounded to the vault, storing claimableDepositShares and claimableDepositAssets. `deposit(assets,...)` computes shares = assets * availableShares / availableAssets (Floor), while `mint(shares,...)` computes assets = shares * availableAssets / availableShares (Floor). Because both use Floor on the user-favorable direction relative to the stored ratio, a controller can repeatedly split claimable assets between `deposit` and `mint` calls to accumulate residual assets that are never consumed (the leftover asset/shares remains claimable while the user already received shares/assets). The rounding direction favors the user in one direction of each conversion, allowing the ratio between claimableDepositShares and claimableDepositAssets to drift in the user's favor and for the last claimant to leave unbacked shares.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker calls requestDeposit(X) with a large X, then investment manager fulfills it, crediting claimableDepositShares≈X*s and claimableDepositAssets=X. 2. Attacker splits the claim across many `deposit` and `mint` calls of varying sizes such that the Rounding.Floor remainder in each call is nonzero, harvesting extra shares relative to `availableShares/availableAssets`. 3. Because `deposit` and `mint` use Floor in opposite ratios, one of them is occasionally favorable to the caller (they can choose which). Attacker drains small amounts from the pool's share backing.
hypotheses.impact: Small but repeatable theft of shares from other depositors; the leftover `claimableDepositShares`/`claimableDepositAssets` becomes inconsistent with the vault's minted balances.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use Ceil rounding against the user on at least one of the two claim functions (mint-direction) so the vault never issues more than the exact proportional amount.

hypotheses.title: deposit()/mint() claim uses stale stored ratio, not current rate
hypotheses.description: When a user claims via deposit(assets, receiver, controller), shares are computed as assets.mulDiv(availableShares, availableAssets, Floor) using the ratio stored at fulfillDeposit time. However, fulfillDeposit already minted shares to the vault based on the rate at fulfillment. If the exchange rate changes between fulfillDeposit and deposit (e.g., due to other fulfillments or investments), the user still gets the originally-minted share count — which is correct — but the claimableDepositAssets/claimableDepositShares ratio can drift from the actual share/asset ratio, causing the last claimer to receive a disproportionate share of the vault's minted shares (dust accumulation or shortfall).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Manager fulfills two deposits at different rates. 2) First user claims partial amount, leaving dust in claimableDepositShares/Assets. 3) Second user claims — the mulDiv ratio no longer matches the actual minted shares, so one user gets more/less than their fair share of the minted shares. 4) The vault may end up holding unmintable shares or a user may be shortchanged.
hypotheses.impact: Dust accumulation in vault, or last claimer receives fewer shares than entitled. Small but systematic value leakage.
hypotheses.recommendation: Store the exact share amount per controller at fulfillDeposit time and let deposit() simply transfer the proportional share of that stored amount, or track shares directly rather than re-deriving from asset ratio.

hypotheses.title: Investment ShareToken balance counted as assets without verifying backing
hypotheses.category: Price used before it is updated / wrong decimals
hypotheses.description: `_calculateInvestmentAssets()` adds `IERC20(investmentShareToken).balanceOf(address(this))` plus `rBalanceOf` to `totalNormalizedAssets`. The investment ShareToken is a separate contract whose share price is not verified against the underlying assets; if the investment ShareToken's own accounting is manipulated (e.g., via direct transfers to its vaults, or if it is a malicious/upgraded contract), the reported `totalNormalizedAssets` is inflated. Since this value feeds `convertNormalizedAssetsToShares`/`convertSharesToNormalizedAssets`, all vault conversions become manipulable.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker manipulates the investment ShareToken's underlying vault balances (e.g., direct transfer to the investment vault) to inflate its share price. 2) `_calculateInvestmentAssets()` returns an inflated value. 3) All vault conversions use the inflated `totalNormalizedAssets`, causing depositors to receive fewer shares and redeemers to receive fewer assets. 4) Attacker redeems at the favorable rate.
hypotheses.impact: Systemic mispricing across all vaults sharing the ShareToken; loss of funds for all users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not rely on the investment ShareToken's raw balance as a proxy for asset value; use a trusted oracle or the investment vault's own `convertToAssets` with a sanity bound, and cap the contribution.

hypotheses.title: withdrawFromInvestment uses previewWithdraw without slippage protection
hypotheses.description: `withdrawFromInvestment` computes `shares = IERC7575($.investmentVault).previewWithdraw(amount)` and then redeems `minShares` (capped at the ShareToken's balance) without any minimum-assets-out check. If the investment vault's share price moves between the preview and the actual redeem (e.g., due to another user's deposit/withdraw or direct transfers), the vault may receive fewer assets than `amount`, and the function silently returns the actual amount. The caller (investment manager) is trusted, but the underlying price manipulation can be performed by an untrusted actor against the investment vault.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pending `withdrawFromInvestment` transaction. 2) Attacker front-runs by depositing/withdrawing in the investment vault or transferring assets directly to it, moving its share price. 3) The vault's redeem yields fewer assets than expected. 4) The shortfall is socialized across all vault users.
hypotheses.impact: Vault receives less than the requested amount; users' redeemable assets are reduced. Loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a `minAssetsOut` parameter and revert if `actualAmount < minAssetsOut`, or use the investment vault's `previewRedeem` with a slippage bound.

hypotheses.title: fulfillDeposit mints shares before updating pending state, enabling reentrancy via share token
hypotheses.category: Ordering / external call before state update
hypotheses.description: `fulfillDeposit()` updates `pendingDepositAssets`, `totalPendingDepositAssets`, `claimableDepositShares`, and `claimableDepositAssets` before calling `ShareTokenUpgradeable.mint(address(this), shares)`. The mint call is an external call to the ShareToken. If the ShareToken (or a future upgrade) has any hook or if the share token is a malicious/upgraded contract, it can re-enter the vault. More importantly, `fulfillDeposits()` (batch) accumulates `shareAmounts` and mints once at the end, but individual state updates happen in the loop; a reentrant call between iterations could observe partially-updated state. The `nonReentrant` guard on the vault blocks re-entry into the vault, but the ShareToken's `mint` is `onlyVaults` and does not itself re-enter the vault, so the primary risk is cross-contract state visibility.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is the investment manager (trusted) — not applicable. 2) Alternatively, if the ShareToken is upgraded to include a hook on `_mint` (e.g., ERC-777-style), the hook can call back into the vault's view functions (`totalAssets`, `getClaimableSharesAndNormalizedAssets`) and observe inconsistent state where `claimableDepositShares` is credited but shares have not yet been minted. 3) An integrator reading these views during the hook gets wrong values.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting observed by integrators; potential for price manipulation if combined with read-only reentrancy.
hypotheses.recommendation: Mint shares before updating claimable state, or ensure the ShareToken's mint cannot trigger callbacks; document that `getClaimableSharesAndNormalizedAssets` must not be read during mint.

hypotheses.title: Zero-amount redeem/withdraw reverts block dust cleanup
hypotheses.description: `redeem()` and `withdraw()` revert on `shares == 0` / `assets == 0`. In `redeem`, if `shares.mulDiv(availableAssets, availableShares, Floor)` rounds to 0 (dust), the user cannot claim the remaining dust because `assets == 0` is not explicitly checked in `redeem` (only `shares == 0`), but `withdraw` reverts on `assets == 0`. More importantly, in `redeem`, if `assets` computes to 0 due to rounding, the function proceeds, burns shares, and skips the transfer (`if (assets > 0)`), effectively burning user shares for nothing. This is a value-loss path rather than a DoS, but the zero-check in `withdraw` prevents dust cleanup.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. User has a tiny claimable redeem amount. 2. User calls `withdraw(0, receiver, controller)` — reverts with `ZeroAssets`. 3. User cannot clean up dust via withdraw. 4. In `redeem`, if `assets` rounds to 0, shares are burned but no assets transferred — user loses shares.
hypotheses.impact: Minor value loss (dust) and inability to clean up small positions.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `redeem`, revert if `assets == 0` before burning shares; in `withdraw`, allow `assets == 0` if it corresponds to a full dust cleanup.

hypotheses.title: requestRedeem transfers shares to vault but does not increase totalClaimableRedeemShares until fulfilled, allowing NF-share accounting drift
hypotheses.description: When a user calls `requestRedeem`, shares move from the user to the vault balance (`vaultTransferFrom`) and are recorded in `pendingRedeemShares`. However `totalClaimableRedeemShares` is only bumped in `fulfillRedeem` (and `totalClaimableRedeemAssets` likewise). `ShareTokenUpgradeable.getCirculatingSupplyAndAssets()` subtracts only `totalClaimableRedeemShares` from supply. Between request and fulfillment, the vault physically holds those shares but they are NOT subtracted from circulating supply. `convertNormalizedAssetsToShares`/`convertSharesToNormalizedAssets` therefore price newly-minted shares against an inflated share supply during that window.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker submits many `requestRedeem` calls across large amounts; these shares sit in vault but do not decrement circulating supply used by conversion math. 2. While requests are pending (before manager can fulfill), attacker calls `requestDeposit` in another asset-vault on the same ShareToken; the deposit gets priced using an inflated denominator (circulatingSupply) because pending-redeem shares are not excluded. 3. Attacker then has the fulfill+claim path executed (or fulfills themselves if manager) to settle, leaving newly-minted deposit shares cheaper than fair, diluting existing holders. Because requests are asynchronous and manager cannot fulfill instantly at scale, the window is available to any attacker with a large deposit ready.
hypotheses.impact: New share issuance is under-priced during the pending redeem window; protocol-wide dilution of ShareToken holders and asset-share accounting drift.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `requestRedeem` (or `ShareTokenUpgradeable`), subtract pending-redeem shares from circulating supply as soon as they are transferred to the vault, not only after `fulfillRedeem`.

hypotheses.title: deposit()/mint() share math uses stale claimable ratio, allows dust griefing
hypotheses.description: `deposit` computes `shares = assets.mulDiv(availableShares, availableAssets, Floor)` using the *stored* claimable ratio, which may diverge from the current ShareToken exchange rate because `fulfillDeposit` minted shares at a different rate. When `availableAssets == assets` the code deletes both claimable fields, but when partial, the ratio is preserved. A user can repeatedly claim tiny amounts to round down to zero shares and revert, or claim in a way that leaves dust that later becomes unclaimable (ZeroSharesCalculated).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User has claimable deposit with assets A and shares S. 2) User calls deposit with assets = A - 1 repeatedly; each call rounds shares down. 3) Eventually availableAssets becomes 1 with availableShares possibly 0 (if rounding consumed all shares), making the remaining claim revert with ZeroSharesCalculated, permanently locking the dust.
hypotheses.impact: User funds (dust) permanently locked in vault; griefing vector.
hypotheses.recommendation: When partial claims leave `availableAssets > 0` but `availableShares == 0`, allow claiming the remaining assets by transferring the residual shares, or use a single stored ratio that cannot diverge.

hypotheses.title: redeem() dust branch deletes state without decrementing totalClaimableRedeemShares
hypotheses.description: In redeem(), when assets == availableAssets, the code deletes claimableRedeemAssets[controller] and claimableRedeemShares[controller] entirely, then decrements totalClaimableRedeemAssets by assets and totalClaimableRedeemShares by shares. But if availableAssets was computed via mulDiv and there is rounding dust (assets < availableAssets due to floor), the branch is not taken and dust remains. More critically, when the branch IS taken, the deleted claimableRedeemShares may be larger than `shares` (the requested amount) if the user requested fewer shares than available but assets happened to equal availableAssets — this can happen when availableShares > shares but mulDiv rounds assets up to availableAssets. The extra shares are silently deleted without being burned, and totalClaimableRedeemShares is only decremented by `shares`, leaving the vault's share balance inconsistent with the tracked total.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User has claimableRedeemShares=100, claimableRedeemAssets=100. 2) User calls redeem(50, ...). assets = 50*100/100 = 50, not equal to availableAssets, so else branch runs — fine. 3) But if availableShares=100, availableAssets=99 (dust from prior rounding), user calls redeem(99, ...): assets = 99*99/100 = 98 (floor), not equal. 4) Edge case: availableShares=100, availableAssets=100, user calls redeem(100,...) — assets=100, branch taken, shares=100, consistent. The real risk is when availableShares > shares but assets==availableAssets due to rounding — then shares burned < shares deleted, leaving orphan shares in vault.
hypotheses.impact: Vault retains shares that are no longer tracked in totalClaimableRedeemShares, causing totalSupply vs circulating supply mismatch and potential accounting drift in getCirculatingSupplyAndAssets.
hypotheses.recommendation: In the branch where assets == availableAssets, burn and decrement by availableShares (not the requested `shares`), or restructure to always decrement by the exact amount deleted.

hypotheses.title: investAssets approves investment vault before deposit, enabling reentrancy via malicious vault
hypotheses.category: External call before state update / reentrancy
hypotheses.description: `investAssets()` calls `IERC20Metadata($.asset).safeIncreaseAllowance($.investmentVault, amount)` and then `IERC7575($.investmentVault).deposit(amount, $.shareToken)`. The investment vault is set by the owner (trusted), but if the investment vault is a malicious or compromised contract (e.g., via a future upgrade or a misconfigured registration), its `deposit` can re-enter the vault. The `nonReentrant` guard blocks re-entry into `investAssets`, but the investment vault could call other vault functions (e.g., `requestDeposit`, `fulfillDeposit`) that are also `nonReentrant` — those would revert. However, the investment vault could call `ShareTokenUpgradeable` functions (e.g., `transfer`, `approve`) or read views. More critically, the allowance is set before the deposit, so a malicious investment vault could pull more than `amount` if the allowance is not reset.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Owner registers a malicious investment vault (requires owner action — out of scope). 2) Alternatively, if the investment vault is upgraded to malicious code, it can call `transferFrom` on the asset using the granted allowance to pull additional funds beyond `amount`. 3) The vault's `totalAssets()` would then be lower than expected, causing accounting errors.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of funds from the vault's asset balance; incorrect accounting in `totalAssets()`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `safeIncreaseAllowance` only for the exact amount and reset allowance to zero after the deposit; or use a pull-based pattern where the investment vault pulls exactly the required amount.

hypotheses.title: claimCancelRedeemRequest transfers shares before removing from pending set
hypotheses.category: Ordering / state update after external call
hypotheses.description: In `claimCancelRedeemRequest()`, the function deletes `claimableCancelRedeemShares[controller]` and removes the controller from `controllersWithPendingRedeemCancelations`, then calls `SafeTokenTransfers.safeTransfer($.shareToken, owner, shares)`. The share token transfer is an external call. If the share token has a hook (e.g., ERC-777-style or a future upgrade), it can re-enter the vault. The `nonReentrant` guard blocks re-entry into the vault, but the share token's `transfer` could call back into the ShareToken's own functions or other vaults. Since the state is already updated, the primary risk is limited, but the ordering still violates strict CEI for the share token interaction.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker uses a share token with a transfer hook (requires share token upgrade — out of scope for untrusted actor). 2) During `safeTransfer`, the hook calls `ShareTokenUpgradeable.getCirculatingSupplyAndAssets` or another vault's view functions. 3) The state is already consistent, so impact is limited.
hypotheses.impact: Minimal — state is updated before the external call, so reentrancy impact is low.
hypotheses.recommendation: No change needed; the current ordering is safe. Consider documenting that the share token must not have transfer hooks.

hypotheses.title: SafeTokenTransfers reverts on zero-amount transfers, blocking dust claims
hypotheses.description: `safeTransfer` and `safeTransferFrom` check `balanceAfter != balanceBefore + amount`. For tokens that revert on zero-amount transfers (some non-standard ERC20s), or for tokens where the recipient is the same as the sender (self-transfer), the balance check may fail. More directly: if `amount == 0`, some tokens revert, and the library does not short-circuit. Combined with the vault's `if (assets > 0)` guard in `redeem`, this is mostly mitigated, but `claimCancelDepositRequest` calls `safeTransfer` unconditionally with `assets` that could theoretically be 0 if state is inconsistent.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. In an edge case where `claimableCancelDepositAssets[controller]` is 0 but the check `assets == 0` is bypassed (it isn't, so this is theoretical). 2. More realistically: a token that reverts on zero transfer causes `safeTransfer` to revert, blocking the claim path.
hypotheses.impact: Potential revert on zero-amount transfers for non-standard tokens, blocking claims.
hypotheses.recommendation: Short-circuit `if (amount == 0) return;` at the top of both functions.

hypotheses.title: permit does not validate owner != address(0), allowing signature for zero address
hypotheses.description: `permit` does not check `owner != address(0)`. If `owner == address(0)`, the nonce for address(0) is consumed, and `_approve(address(0), spender, value)` is called. This sets an allowance for address(0), which is harmless. However, it consumes the nonce for address(0), which could be used in a future exploit. Low severity.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker calls permit with owner = address(0). 2. Nonce for address(0) is consumed. 3. No direct impact.
hypotheses.impact: Nonce for address(0) is consumed, but no funds are at risk.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (owner == address(0)) revert ERC20InvalidApprover(address(0));` at the start of permit.

hypotheses.title: withdraw() in ERC7575VaultUpgradeable does not check if shares > 0 before burning
hypotheses.description: `withdraw` calculates `shares = assets.mulDiv(availableShares, availableAssets, Math.Rounding.Floor)`. If `shares == 0`, the burn is skipped (`if (shares > 0)`). But the assets are still transferred. This means a user can withdraw assets without burning any shares if the rounding results in 0 shares. This is a dust attack: repeatedly withdraw small amounts to drain assets without burning shares. However, the user must have claimable redeem assets, which come from a prior redeem request where shares were transferred to the vault. So the user already paid shares. The dust is just rounding. Low severity.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. User requests redeem with a large amount of shares. 2. fulfillRedeem converts to assets. 3. User calls withdraw with a tiny amount of assets. 4. shares = 0 due to rounding. 5. Assets are transferred, no shares burned. 6. Repeat to drain assets without burning shares.
hypotheses.impact: User can drain assets without burning proportional shares, but the amounts are tiny (dust). Low impact.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `shares > 0` in withdraw, or handle dust by burning at least 1 share.

hypotheses.title: totalAssets() excludes totalCancelDepositAssets but claimCancelDepositRequest uses physical balance
hypotheses.description: `totalAssets()` subtracts `totalPendingDepositAssets + totalClaimableRedeemAssets + totalCancelDepositAssets` from the vault's asset balance. However, assets moved to `pendingCancelDepositAssets` (via `cancelDepositRequest`) are still counted inside `totalPendingDepositAssets`-derived bookkeeping until the fulfillment step, then moved to `claimableCancelDepositAssets` while `totalCancelDepositAssets` tracks them. If cancel fulfillment ordering is chosen (e.g., cancelDepositRequest then immediately cancelDepositRequest again after fulfillCancelDepositRequest but before claim), a controller can have both `pendingCancelDepositAssets` (still counted in `totalCancelDepositAssets`) and the underlying physical assets also included in `totalAssets()` — actually the opposite: after cancelDepositRequest, physical assets remain in the vault but totalAssets subtracts them; investment manager can then call `investAssets(totalAssets())` and move remaining "free" assets. Combined with the fact that `investAssets` uses `totalAssets()` (which already excludes cancel reserves) as the availability cap, redeemed-from-investment flows can be timed to bypass reserved cancel liquidity.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker with multiple controllers calls `cancelDepositRequest` on each, inflating `totalCancelDepositAssets`. 2. `totalAssets()` now under-reports free balance, so `investAssets` is limited. 3. Attacker prepares an `investAssets` call with the pre-cancel amount; before fulfillment of cancels they call `withdrawFromInvestment` to bring back liquidity; since `totalAssets()` reflects only free balance while physical balance is larger, the attacker can arrange a call ordering where pending cancel assets subsidize their own invested back-and-forth. Net effect: cancel reserves may be depleted while `claimableCancelDepositAssets` still promises payouts.
hypotheses.impact: Cancel obligations (claimableCancelDepositAssets) may be unbacked at claim time if manager invests reserves; combined with any reordering of fulfill/invest, ERC7887 claimants can find the vault short on assets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure cancel claims are covered by reserving asset liquidity in a separate pool that `investAssets` explicitly cannot touch, and reconsider using `totalAssets()` as an investment availability ceiling while cancel reserves are nonzero.

hypotheses.title: cancelDepositRequest blocks new deposits but not new redeems for same controller
hypotheses.description: `cancelDepositRequest` adds the controller to `controllersWithPendingDepositCancelations`, which blocks new `requestDeposit` calls, but does not block `requestRedeem`. Conversely, `cancelRedeemRequest` blocks new redeems but not new deposits. A controller can therefore have a pending deposit cancelation and simultaneously submit a redeem request, or vice versa, creating interleaved state that the ERC7887 spec intends to prevent (blocking new requests while cancelation is pending).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User calls requestDeposit, then cancelDepositRequest (now blocked from new deposits). 2) User calls requestRedeem for shares they still hold. 3) Manager fulfills both; user ends up with both a claimable cancel-deposit and a claimable redeem, potentially double-counting assets in `totalAssets` accounting or confusing the manager's fulfillment logic.
hypotheses.impact: Inconsistent state; potential accounting confusion; spec deviation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Block both deposit and redeem requests while any cancelation is pending for the controller, or explicitly document and enforce the intended cross-blocking semantics.
